**George Elmer Pataki** ([/p ə ˈ t ɑː k i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born June 24, 1945) is an American politician who served as the 53rd [governor of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_York "Governor of New York") from 1995 to 2006. He previously served in the [State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature") from 1985 to 1994, and as mayor of [Peekskill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peekskill,_New_York "Peekskill, New York") from 1981 to 1984. Pataki was the third elected [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") governor of New York since 1923, after [Thomas E. Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_E._Dewey "Thomas E. Dewey") and [Nelson Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller "Nelson Rockefeller"), and is currently the most recent one.

Pataki's most notable achievements as governor included the creation of a number of new [health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care "Health care") programs, presiding over recovery efforts following the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"), and for increasing the state's credit rating three times. He chose not to run for a fourth term in [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2006 New York gubernatorial election"), being succeeded by Democrat [Eliot Spitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Spitzer "Eliot Spitzer"). Pataki and [Mary Donohue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Donohue "Mary Donohue") (his second Lt. Governor) are the last Republicans elected to statewide office in New York, although Republicans [Joseph Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bruno "Joseph Bruno") and [Dean Skelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Skelos "Dean Skelos") each briefly served as acting Lieutenant Governor in 2008.

Pataki announced his candidacy for the Republican Party presidential nomination on May 28, 2015. He withdrew from the race shortly before the primaries began on December 29, 2015.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Pataki was born on June 24, 1945[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-PatakiBorn1945.NYT1994-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-PatakiBorn1945.NYT98-2) in [Peekskill, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peekskill,_New_York "Peekskill, New York"). Pataki's paternal grandfather[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-NYT-3) was Pataki János (known in the U.S. as _John Pataki_, 1883–1971) of [Aranyosapáti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aranyosap%C3%A1ti "Aranyosapáti"), [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-NYT-3) The family name's [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language") pronunciation is [['pɒtɒki]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Hungarian "Help:IPA/Hungarian") and means "from the creek (little river)." János came to the United States in 1908, worked in a hat factory and had married Erzsébet (later Elizabeth; 1887–1975), also Hungarian-born, around 1904. Their son, Pataki's father, was Louis P. Pataki (1912–1996), a [mailman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail_carrier "Mail carrier") and volunteer fire chief, who ran the Pataki Farm.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-4) Pataki's maternal grandfather was Matteo Laganà (born in [Calabria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabria "Calabria"), Italy in 1889), who married Agnes Lynch of [County Louth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Louth "County Louth"), Ireland around 1914. Their daughter, Margaret Lagana (1915–2017), was Pataki's mother. Pataki has an older brother, Louis. Pataki speaks some [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-NYT-3) as well as Spanish, French, and German.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-5)

After graduating from [Peekskill High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peekskill_High_School "Peekskill High School"), Pataki entered [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") in 1963 on an academic [scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship "Scholarship") and graduated in 1967 with a history major.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-PatakiBorn1945.NYT1994-1) While there, Pataki was [Chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairperson "Chairperson") of the Conservative Party of the [Yale Political Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Political_Union "Yale Political Union"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-6) where he participated in debates, and a member of the conservative [Calliopean Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calliopean_Society "Calliopean Society").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-ABurnsNYTimes05282015-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-8) He received his [J.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") from [Columbia Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Law_School "Columbia Law School") in 1970.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-9)

While practicing law at Plunkett and Jaffe, P.C. in Peekskill, Pataki became friends with [Michael C. Finnegan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_C._Finnegan "Michael C. Finnegan"), who would go on to be the architect of Pataki's ascendancy to power.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-finn1-10) Finnegan would go on to manage Pataki's campaigns for Mayor, [State Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Assembly "New York State Assembly"), [State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Senate "New York State Senate"), and the governorship.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-finn3-11) Finnegan was then appointed chief counsel to the governor in 1995, and played the key role in developing and negotiating nearly all of Pataki's early legislative success.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-finn2-12)

### Mayor of Peekskill

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mayor of Peekskill")]

Pataki first won elected office in November 1981. He was elected mayor of the city of Peekskill, which is located in the northwestern part of Westchester County. Pataki defeated Democratic incumbent Fred Bianco Jr., winning 70% of the vote. In November 1983, he was re-elected mayor, winning 74% of the vote.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-PatakiBorn1945.NYT98-2)

### New York State Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: New York State Assembly")]

In November 1984, Pataki was elected to the New York State Assembly (91st District), by defeating one-term Democratic incumbent William J. Ryan, winning 53% of the vote. In November 1986, Pataki defeated Ryan in a rematch, capturing 63% of the vote. Pataki won a third term in November 1988, winning 74% of the vote against Democratic candidate Mark Zinna. Pataki won a fourth and final term in November 1990, winning over 90% of the vote, as he only faced a minor party candidate. He was an assemblyman in the [186th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/186th_New_York_State_Legislature "186th New York State Legislature"), [187th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/187th_New_York_State_Legislature "187th New York State Legislature"), [188th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/188th_New_York_State_Legislature "188th New York State Legislature") and [189th New York State Legislatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/189th_New_York_State_Legislature "189th New York State Legislature").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-:0-13)

### New York State Senate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: New York State Senate")]

From 1983 to 1992, the 91st Assembly district included parts of Westchester, Orange, Rockland, and Putnam Counties. However, in 1992, Assembly Democrats substantially redrew the district boundaries, placing the newly renamed 90th Assembly district entirely within [Westchester County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County,_New_York "Westchester County, New York"). Instead of running in the newly redrawn district, Pataki decided to challenge seven-term incumbent [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") State Senator [Mary B. Goodhue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_B._Goodhue "Mary B. Goodhue") in a Republican primary in Senate District 37 by criticizing her for taking her grandchildren to Disney World and missing a vote in [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York"). Pataki won the primary by a 52% to 48% margin. However, Goodhue still planned to appear on the November ballot on a minor party line. In November 1992, Pataki won the general election. He served in the Senate during the [190th New York State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/190th_New_York_State_Legislature "190th New York State Legislature") and ran for governor at the next election.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-:0-13)

## Gubernatorial campaigns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Gubernatorial campaigns")]

### 1994 campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1994 campaign")]

Main article: [1994 New York gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1994 New York gubernatorial election")

Pataki was a first-term state senator from [Westchester County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County,_New_York "Westchester County, New York") when he launched his bid for the Republican nomination for governor in 1994. He said he launched the campaign because of his frustration in the Senate regarding how [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York") worked and on tax issues. Pataki's campaign received a boost when he was endorsed by U.S. Sen. [Al D'Amato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_D'Amato "Al D'Amato").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-Pataki_AL_D_Patron.NYT1997-14) He received the party's endorsement at the spring state convention and easily defeated former State Republican Chairman Richard Rosenbaum in the September primary. Pataki was considered an underdog from the start since he was running against three-term Gov. [Mario Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cuomo "Mario Cuomo") and because Pataki had little name recognition statewide. D'Amato reportedly backed Pataki because of a poll that showed a [pro-choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-choice "Pro-choice"), fiscal conservative from the New York City suburbs could win statewide for governor. The poll also showed a female running mate for [lieutenant governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_New_York "Lieutenant Governor of New York") would help the ticket. Academic [Betsy McCaughey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_McCaughey "Betsy McCaughey") was chosen as Pataki's running mate.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-15)

The polls had Governor Cuomo ahead by as many as ten points going into the final two weeks, but they narrowed at the end. Pataki made an issue of Cuomo seeking a fourth term as governor and pledged to serve only two terms in office. Cuomo was helped late in the race by the endorsement of New York City Mayor [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-16) Pataki narrowly defeated Cuomo in the general election. Many, including Pataki himself, believed [Howard Stern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Stern "Howard Stern")'s endorsement of Pataki was a major reason for his win.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-17) He finished with 48.8% of the vote to Cuomo's 45.5%, and independence candidate [Tom Golisano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Golisano "Tom Golisano") finished with 4.2%.

Pataki made up for a soft performance in New York City by running up a decisive margin outside of it, especially among upstaters disenchanted with Cuomo. Pataki won all but one county outside the Five Boroughs.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-18) Pataki became New York's first elected Republican governor since Nelson Rockefeller.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-19)

### 1998 campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1998 campaign")]

Main article: [1998 New York gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1998 New York gubernatorial election")

Pataki was considered the front-runner from the start of the 1998 campaign for governor.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He was unopposed for the Republican nomination[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and paired with a new running mate, Judge [Mary Donohue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Donohue "Mary Donohue").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-paired-20) The Democrats faced a primary battle between New York City Council Speaker [Peter Vallone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Vallone "Peter Vallone"), Lt. Gov. [Betsy McCaughey Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_McCaughey_Ross "Betsy McCaughey Ross"), who had switched parties, and former Transportation Commissioner James LaRocca. Vallone captured the Democratic nomination, with [Thomas Golisano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Golisano "Thomas Golisano") running as the Independence nominee and McCaughey Ross as the Liberal Party nominee. Pataki was easily reelected to a second term in office.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-21) He finished with 54.3% of the vote, his highest percentage finish in a gubernatorial race, to Vallone's 33.2% and Golisano's 7.7%.

### 2002 campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2002 campaign")]

Main article: [2002 New York gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2002 New York gubernatorial election")

Pataki was considered a strong contender for a third term, despite having pledged in 1994 to serve only two terms. He ran again on a ticket with Lt. Gov. Mary Donohue and the Democrats faced a primary battle between State Comptroller [Carl McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_McCall "Carl McCall") and former HUD Secretary [Andrew Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cuomo "Andrew Cuomo"), Mario Cuomo's son. Pataki emphasized his previous work and the need to have continuity following Sept. 11.

McCall essentially secured the Democratic nomination when Andrew Cuomo stumbled (and ultimately withdrew before the primary at the urging of his mentor [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")); Cuomo was quoted in the media as saying, regarding Pataki's performance post-9/11:

> Pataki stood behind the leader. He held the leader's coat. He was a great assistant to the leader. But he was not a leader. Cream rises to the top, and Rudy Giuliani rose to the top.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-22)

Pataki sought the nomination of the [Independence Party of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Party_of_New_York "Independence Party of New York") in his bid for a third term as well. He faced the party's founder and 1994 and 1998 nominee, [Thomas Golisano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Golisano "Tom Golisano"), in his bid for the nomination.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-23) Pataki ran an active primary campaign and lost to Golisano. Donohue did win the primary for lieutenant governor and was the running mate of both Pataki and Golisano in the general election.

In the general election, Pataki defeated McCall and Golisano easily.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-24) As in 1998 due to Golisano's presence on the ballot, Pataki did not win a majority, instead winning a plurality. Pataki won 49.4% of the vote, and McCall only mustered 33.5% with wins in four of the five New York City boroughs. Golisano finished with the highest vote total of his political career, and the highest vote total for any candidate of the [Independence Party of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Party_of_New_York "Independence Party of New York") in any statewide election.

This was the last time a Republican was elected [Governor of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_York "Governor of New York"), and the last time a Republican has cracked over 41% in a gubernatorial election until the 2022 election in which Republican candidate Congressman [Lee Zeldin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Zeldin "Lee Zeldin") amassed 47% of the vote against incumbent Democrat [Kathy Hochul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Hochul "Kathy Hochul").

### Retirement from the governorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Retirement from the governorship")]

By the summer of 2005, opinion polls indicated that Pataki would face an uphill battle if he sought a fourth term in 2006. Accordingly, he announced on July 27, 2005, that he would not do so, saying that New York was "a better state than it was 10 years ago" and that he was retiring so he could "follow a new path, find new challenges."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-25) He was succeeded by Democrat [Eliot Spitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Spitzer "Eliot Spitzer").

As Governor of New York, Pataki was known as a moderate to liberal Republican who cut taxes and was tough on crime, but who also supported gun control, environmental protection, gay rights, and abortion rights.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-Perry-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-30)

### Fiscal policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Fiscal policy")]

#### Taxes, spending, budget power, and economic growth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Taxes, spending, budget power, and economic growth")]

Under the Pataki Administration, New York's credit rating was increased three times by [Moody's Investors Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody's_Investors_Service "Moody's Investors Service"), a fact that he highlighted often before his critics.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-31) During his three terms in office, he introduced and approved more tax cuts than any of his predecessors. Following through on a campaign promise, Pataki led a push to cut both the individual and the corporate tax rates in New York. The state's infamously high income tax rates dropped by 20% on average, but an economic downturn following the attacks of September 11 and increasing state spending caused [Sheldon Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheldon_Silver "Sheldon Silver") and [Joseph Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bruno "Joseph Bruno") to coordinate an effort to roll back a number of these cuts in 2003 over Pataki's veto power.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-32)

The STAR and STAR-Plus programs were also introduced during Pataki's governorship. The STAR program introduced tax relief for New York's homeowners and landowners on their school taxes. The STAR-Plus program was later introduced when relief was diminished by increasing school taxes, increasing spending and State Aid.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-33) In his third term Pataki challenged the Speaker of the Assembly, resulting in two Court of Appeals decisions sustaining the powers of the governor to formulate a statewide budget.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-34)

### Social policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Social policy")]

#### Abortion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Abortion")]

Pataki describes himself as [pro-choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-choice "Pro-choice").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-ABurnsNYTimes05282015-7) In 1999, he called upon the Republican Party to soften its platform language regarding opposition to abortion rights.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-Perry-26)

#### Gay rights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Gay rights")]

Pataki lobbied heavily in favor of the [Sexual Orientation Non-Discrimination Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_Orientation_Non-Discrimination_Act "Sexual Orientation Non-Discrimination Act"), a [gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_rights "Gay rights") bill[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-ABurnsNYTimes05282015-7) that had languished in the state Senate for many years due to the opposition of Senate Leader [Joseph Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bruno "Joseph Bruno"). In late 2002, Bruno finally gave in; the bill passed the Senate and was signed into law by Pataki.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-37) He opposed [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage") as governor.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-38)

#### Crime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Crime")]

Polls showed that the majority of New Yorkers wanted the state's death penalty laws restored. Prior to Pataki's tenure, a bill to restore the death penalty had passed the Legislature for several years in a row only to be vetoed by [Mario Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cuomo "Mario Cuomo"). Pataki made the issue a top priority of his, and when the bill reached his desk in 1995, he signed it into law. The [New York Court of Appeals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Court_of_Appeals "New York Court of Appeals") later ruled the death penalty law unconstitutional in a 4–3 decision in [People v. LaValle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_v._LaValle "People v. LaValle") (2004).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-39)

Being tough on crime was a major plank of Pataki's campaign for governor. In 2011, the administration touted statistics that illustrated that crime had steadily reduced during the 12 years Pataki had been governor, bringing New York from the 6th most dangerous state in the nation to the 7th safest.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-40) During his time in office, he signed into law over 100 new bills to change New York's criminal statutes. In 2000, Pataki helped lead the legislature in passing some of the then-strictest [gun control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_control "Gun control") laws in the country.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-41) Numerous aspects of the bill had been put forward by members of the Democratic-controlled Assembly but had never made it through the Republican held Senate. With numerous mass shootings in recent public memory, he urged a number of Republican Senators to support the bill, eventually passing it in a bipartisan effort. His administration also launched programs such as SAF-T (Statewide Anti-Fugitive Teams) and the 100 Most Wanted.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-42) The initiatives were aimed at disseminating descriptions of criminals who were evading law enforcement officials to promote the ability of average citizens to help aid in their capture. Versions of [Megan's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan's_Law "Megan's Law") and [Kendra's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendra's_Law "Kendra's Law") were integrated into New York's laws under the governor as well as a number of reforms to the [Rockefeller Drug Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Drug_Laws "Rockefeller Drug Laws").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-44) The changes to the Rockefeller laws were largely focused on inmates' ability to appeal for an early release from sentences that were passed on them under mandatory minimum sentencing statutes.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-45)

#### Health care

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Health care")]

Under the Pataki Administration a number of new health care programs were created focusing on expanding care to the state's poorest citizens. In 1999, Governor Pataki signed into law comprehensive health care legislation that provided health insurance coverage, under Family Health Plus, to lower income adults who do not have health insurance through their employers. Child Health plus greatly expanded coverage for poorer families with children under 19 who did not qualify for [Medicaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid "Medicaid").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-46) By 2001, 530,000 children had been enrolled in the program.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-nytimes.com-47) Family Health Plus would expand insurance coverage even further, offering free insurance to families and single adults who had too much income to be covered by Medicaid but could not afford insurance.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-nytimes.com-47) Pataki also increased the affordability and availability of medication for seniors under New York's [EPIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elderly_Pharmaceutical_Insurance_Coverage "Elderly Pharmaceutical Insurance Coverage") program by lowering fees and expanding eligibility.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-48) New York's 2003 ban on smoking in public places was passed and signed into law under the Pataki administration in the hopes that it would promote better health in New York and reduce health care cost over time.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-49) Assessing his twelve years in office, _The New York Times_ ran an editorial praising his work on health care.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-nyt-legacy-50)

#### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Environment")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/US_Navy_020907-N-3399W-001_SECNAV_announces_naming_of_USS_New_York_%28LPD_21%29.jpg/250px-US_Navy_020907-N-3399W-001_SECNAV_announces_naming_of_USS_New_York_%28LPD_21%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_020907-N-3399W-001_SECNAV_announces_naming_of_USS_New_York_(LPD_21).jpg)

George Pataki at the [USS _New York_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_New_York_(LPD_21) "USS New York (LPD 21)"), September 7, 2002 (back row, left)

In 2005, _[BusinessWeek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Businessweek "Businessweek")_ placed George Pataki among the 20 individuals it commended for their personal efforts to combat global warming, citing his Greenhouse Gas Task Force and efforts to increase New York's usage of renewable energies.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-51) In 1996, Pataki oversaw the creation and passage of the Clean Water/Clean Air Environmental Bond Act. The act put forth $1.75 billion for over 2,200 environmentally minded projects throughout the state.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-52) Projects were focused on improving drinking water quality, closing landfills, investing in recycling programs, cleaning up New York's polluted waterways, funding cleanup of [Brownfields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownfields "Brownfields") and clean-air projects.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-53) During his tenure, Pataki added over one million acres to the entirety of the protected open spaces of New York.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-54) He also worked to protect the drinking water of millions of New Yorkers through the Catskill Watershed Agreement.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-55) Through the agreement, the numerous small communities that surround the 19 reservoirs that provide drinking water for New York City received $1 billion in aid to assuage environmental issues and promote local development in return for accepting higher standards of environmental regulations to better protect the reservoirs. On Pataki's final day in office, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ ran an editorial evaluating his twelve years as governor and praised his work on the environment.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-nyt-legacy-50)

#### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Education")]

Pataki heeded mounting desire to allow New York to join numerous other states in the growing movement for charter schools.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-56) In 1998, Pataki prevailed upon the Legislature to pass a charter school law by threatening to veto a legislative pay raise if the bill was not passed.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-57) Over the course of his terms in office, Pataki would expand the availability of charter schools in New York City and raise the state's cap on charter schools to 250.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-58)

In coordination with Mayor [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani"), Pataki pushed to begin disassembling the reputation of [City University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_University_of_New_York "City University of New York") system as a group of remedial schools.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-59) Starting in 1999, CUNY colleges would be required to drop their remedial courses over a 3-year period and restrict students who could not pass entry exams in an effort to deliver a higher quality college education through the city colleges. Pataki also put forth legislation that would lend mayors in New York's five largest cities greater control over their education systems.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-60) Through negotiations this authority was only awarded to the mayor of New York City as an attempt to overcome a system of school boards that many considered to be hampering efforts at reform.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-61)

## Post-governorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Post-governorship")]

After leaving the governorship, Pataki joined the law firm [Chadbourne & Parke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chadbourne_&_Parke "Chadbourne & Parke") in New York[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-74) joining their [renewable energy practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_energy_law "New York energy law"). He continued to flirt with a possible bid for president. After ruling out a presidential campaign, Pataki retained his [political action committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee"), which he could legally use to further his own views and other political interests.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-75) In addition, Pataki has formed an environmental consulting firm with his former chief of staff John Cahill, the Pataki-Cahill Group.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-auto1-76)

Pataki holds an [amateur radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio "Amateur radio") license.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-77)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Governor George E. Pataki Leadership and Learning Center")]

The Governor George E. Pataki Leadership and Learning Center, located in [Peekskill, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peekskill,_New_York "Peekskill, New York"), is designed to educate schoolchildren on government using Governor Pataki's public service as an example.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-The_New_York_Times-78)[Charles A. Gargano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_A._Gargano "Charles A. ### 2016 presidential campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: 2016 presidential campaign")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Pataki_for_President_Campaign_Logo.png/250px-Pataki_for_President_Campaign_Logo.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pataki_for_President_Campaign_Logo.png)

Pataki's campaign logo

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/George_Pataki_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg/250px-George_Pataki_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:George_Pataki_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg)

Pataki speaking before the Iowa Republican Party in Des Moines, Iowa, in May 2015.

In early 2015, Pataki started exploring a candidacy for the [2016 Republican presidential nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_presidential_primaries,_2016 "Republican Party presidential primaries, 2016");[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-88) On May 28, 2015, Pataki formally announced his campaign for the 2016 Republican nomination.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-90) He had previously considered running in 2008[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-91) and in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election "2012 United States presidential election"),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-92) but had decided against it.

Pataki's candidacy was considered a long-shot because of his age, because he had not run for office since 2002, and because of his liberal stances on abortion, gun control and environmental protection.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-94) Pataki received the endorsements of two New Hampshire State Senators: [John Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Reagan_(New_Hampshire_politician) "John Reagan (New Hampshire politician)")[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-politico.com-95) and [Nancy Stiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Stiles "Nancy Stiles").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-politico.com-95)

Pataki's run failed to gain traction. He failed to make the main stage in the candidate debates, being [relegated to the undercard debates or being excluded altogether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_debates_2016 "Republican debates 2016"). His national poll numbers [stayed in the one percent range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationwide_opinion_polling_for_the_Republican_Party_2016_presidential_primaries "Nationwide opinion polling for the Republican Party 2016 presidential primaries"). Pataki did not file to be on the primary ballot in multiple states and missed the filing deadlines for Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah, and Virginia.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-98)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-100) On December 29, 2015, Pataki ended his campaign before the Republican presidential primaries had begun.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-Pataki_PresRun.NYT2015-102) He endorsed Florida Senator [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio") on January 26, 2016[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-103) and went on to endorse Ohio Governor [John Kasich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kasich "John Kasich") after Rubio suspended his campaign.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-104)

After video footage of eventual nominee [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump")[making lewd comments about women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Access_Hollywood_tape "Donald Trump Access Hollywood tape") emerged on October 7, 2016, Pataki described the Republican nominee's candidacy as "a poisonous mix of bigotry & ignorance." Pataki also called upon Trump to step down as the Republican nominee.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-105)

### 2020 presidential election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: 2020 presidential election")]

In 2020, he declined to endorse [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") for re-election. He stopped short of endorsing [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), citing disagreements with foreign policy relating to U.S.-China relations.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-106) Pataki opposed efforts to decertify the election results.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-107)

### 2022 New York gubernatorial election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: 2022 New York gubernatorial election")]

In September 2022, Pataki endorsed Republican candidate [Lee Zeldin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Zeldin "Lee Zeldin") for Governor of New York, against incumbent Democrat [Kathy Hochul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Hochul "Kathy Hochul").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-108) Zeldin went on to lose the [election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2022 New York gubernatorial election") by 6.4%, the closest margin since Pataki's [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1994 New York gubernatorial election") win.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Pataki&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Pataki married his wife, Libby, in 1973. The Patakis have four children.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-auto-109)

Pataki is [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-auto-109)

Pataki suffered a burst [appendix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermiform_appendix "Vermiform appendix") and had an emergency [appendectomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appendectomy "Appendectomy") on February 16, 2006, at Hudson Valley Hospital Center. Six days later, he developed a post-surgical complication ([bowel obstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowel_obstruction "Bowel obstruction") caused by [adhesions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adhesion_(medicine) "Adhesion (medicine)"))[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-111) and was transferred to [New York-Presbyterian/Columbia University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NewYork-Presbyterian_Hospital "NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital") for a second operation. From there, he was discharged on March 6.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki#cite_note-112)

steps.text:
The first time a Republican won the New York gubernatorial election was in 1994 when **George Pataki** was elected governor.  
On the 1994 ballot he appeared on three lines – the U.S. Republican Line, the Conservative Party Line, and the Tax Cut Now Line 【4†L7-L12】.  These were the parties that ran under when Pataki won and—by extension, the parties under which he would have served as governor.
